title: India Must Beat the Unbeaten: A Lord's Date With Australia Will Decide Their World Cup
excerpt: Australia have won every match and can afford to lose; India cannot. Sunday's group finale at Lord's is, in effect, a quarterfinal India have to win to reach the last four.
body:
For two weeks the ICC Women's T20 World Cup in England has felt like a tournament with one inevitability and a scramble for everything else. Australia, the six-time champions, have won all four of their matches and carry a net run rate — plus 4.724 — that reads less like a statistic than a warning. Everyone else has been playing for the three semi-final places left over. On Sunday at Lord's, India arrive at the front of that queue, and they must get past the one team nobody has been able to touch.

The fixture is the second half of a Group A double-header at the home of cricket, and the equation is brutally simple for Harmanpreet Kaur's side. Win, and India are almost certainly through to the last four. Lose, and they are dependent on results elsewhere and on the cold arithmetic of run rate. Former India batter Aakash Chopra called it bluntly: "It would be a virtual quarterfinal. Beat Australia at Lord's and make a place in the semifinals."

## How India Got Here

India began the campaign in control, beating Pakistan and the Netherlands to open with two points apiece and a healthy run rate. Then came the stumble — a six-wicket defeat to South Africa at Old Trafford that turned a comfortable-looking group into a knife-edge. In that game India won the toss, batted, and could only manage 158 for 7, unable to convert a fast start into the kind of total that wins World Cup knockouts.


![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)



> **"Former India batter Aakash Chopra called it bluntly: "It would be a virtual quarterfinal."**



A must-win against Bangladesh steadied the ship. Shafali Verma, restored to her belligerent best, top-scored as India chased down a competitive target with five wickets in hand to stay alive. It was the innings of a player who has spent this tournament reminding selectors why her ceiling is so high — 31 off 15 against South Africa, then a half-century when it mattered most against Bangladesh.

That win left the table finely poised heading into the final round. Australia sit top on eight points, India and South Africa level on six, with Bangladesh trailing on four. The last group fixtures — Bangladesh against South Africa, then Australia against India, both at Lord's on Sunday — will settle three semi-final places in an afternoon.

## The Australia Problem

There is no gentle way to frame the task. Australia have been the most complete side in the tournament by a distance. They opened with a 65-run win over the 2024 finalists South Africa, beat Bangladesh by nine wickets, dismantled the Netherlands by 98 runs, and then produced an all-round masterclass from Ellyse Perry to thrash Pakistan by 113 runs.


![Harmanpreet Kaur — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/38/Harmanpreet_Kaur_with_2025_Women%27s_Cricket_World_Cup_trophy.jpg)


Their net run rate is so far ahead that Australia can lose to India on Sunday and still progress to the semi-finals. India enjoy no such cushion. For India to leapfrog the Australians on net run rate — the doomsday scenario that would only matter if three teams finish level on eight points — they would need to win by something like 91 runs, or chase a target down with roughly 11 overs to spare. Those are not realistic margins against this Australian side. The message for India is therefore uncomplicated: win the match, and the calculators can stay in the bag.

## What India Need to Get Right

India's batting has flickered rather than blazed. Smriti Mandhana, one of the finest white-ball openers in the world, has yet to produce the defining innings the tournament has been waiting for, and India have leaned heavily on Shafali's fast starts. Captain Harmanpreet Kaur, a Lord's centurion in the 2017 50-over World Cup semi-final against Australia, knows better than most what a knockout occasion at this ground can do for a career — and a country.

The bowling has had its moments, with left-arm spinner N Shree Charani striking early blows in the powerplay, including a double-wicket maiden against South Africa that removed Proteas captain Laura Wolvaardt. Against Australia's deep, aggressive batting order, India will need that new-ball control to hold for far longer than 20 deliveries.

## Why the Diaspora Should Watch

For Indian fans in London, New York, Toronto and Sydney, Sunday is more than a fixture — it is a window into how far the women's game has travelled. A women's World Cup match at Lord's, broadcast across time zones, is the kind of stage that did not exist for India's women a generation ago. Many in the diaspora grew up watching the men's team chase these moments; their daughters now have Mandhana, Shafali and Harmanpreet to follow, in a tournament that is finally being treated as the marquee event it is.

The schedule does India no favours — beating Australia is the hardest assignment in the women's game right now. But it is also the most direct route to the semi-finals, and the cleanest way to announce that this Indian side belongs in the last four on merit, not on mathematics. The first ball is due at 2:30pm BST on Sunday. After two weeks of one-sided certainty, the tournament has finally produced a contest India cannot afford to lose.
